issues.legal_issue: A statutory bar on challenging alienations for being contrary to custom applies to pending challenges, including those before an appellate court, even when the alienation occurred before the bar took effect.
material_facts: The appellants were challenging alienations on the ground that they were contrary to custom under the law governing customary challenges.
When the 1973 amendment took effect, the challenges were still pending at the appellate stage.
The amendment provided that no person could contest an alienation on the ground that it was contrary to custom.
Earlier decisions had applied the amendment to pending proceedings, while another decision had questioned that approach.
issues.conclusion: The amended bar applied to all pending actions, whether at trial or on appeal. Applying it to a pending challenge did not make it retrospective as to the earlier alienation; the right to contest continued only until final decision and was then unavailable.
issues.legal_principle: Section 7 of the Punjab Custom (Power to Contest) Act, 1920, as amended by the Punjab Custom (Power to Contest) Amendment Act, 1973, bars custom-based challenges to alienations. Although section 1(2) fixes the amendment's commencement, the text and purpose show that the bar governs pending proceedings. An appeal is a continuation of the suit, and the contest continues until final decision. The Court relied on Thakur Gokulchand v. Parvin Kumari, Garikapatti Veeraya v. N. Subbiah Choudhury, Lakshmi Narayan Guin v. Niranjan Modak, Dayawati v. Inderjit, and other authorities on changes in law during pending proceedings; it confirmed the approach in Ujaggar Singh v. Dharam Singh and Udham Singh v. Tarsem Singh and did not accept the contrary concern expressed in Bara Singh v. Kashmira Singh. The Court distinguished retroactive application to pending proceedings from retrospective operation upon the earlier transaction, applying the principles in Rafiquennessa v. Lal Bahadur Chetri and Athlumney, Ex parte Wilson.

predicates.custom_based_alienation_challenge: A person brought a proceeding to challenge an alienation on the ground that it was contrary to custom.
predicates.challenge_pending_when_legal_bar_took_ef: The challenge had not received a final decision when the legal bar took effect.
predicates.legal_bar_prohibits_custom_based_challen: A legal change took effect providing that persons could no longer contest alienations on the ground that they were contrary to custom.

issues.definition: When a custom-based alienation challenge remains pending as a legal bar against such challenges takes effect, the challenge is unavailable.

issues.legal_issue: Ending the customary right to challenge alienations does not extinguish independent rights to challenge them under Hindu law, and the Hindu Succession Act alone did not displace customary restrictions on alienation that it did not address.
material_facts: Customary rules in Punjab restricted some alienations of ancestral property and allowed certain descendants or collaterals to challenge them.
The Punjab Laws Act, 1872 and the Punjab Custom (Power to Contest) Act, 1920 recognized and regulated aspects of custom-based challenges.
The Hindu Succession Act dealt with succession matters but did not appear to abrogate customary restrictions on alienation by a male proprietor beyond those under Hindu law.
The 1973 amendment was enacted to end the right to contest alienations on the ground that they were contrary to custom.
issues.conclusion: The 1973 amendment did away with the custom-based right to contest, but the parties' rights under Hindu law remained unaffected. The Hindu Succession Act had not itself abolished the relevant customary rules on alienation, and an independent Hindu-law challenge remained available for consideration.
issues.legal_principle: Section 4 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 overrides inconsistent existing rules in matters dealt with by that Act; it does not abrogate rules on matters it does not address. The Punjab Laws Act, 1872, section 5, provided for custom as a rule of decision, while sections 6 and 7 of the Punjab Custom (Power to Contest) Act, 1920, and its 1973 amendment addressed the right to contest alienations. The Court distinguished a custom that is judicially noticed or legally confirmed and regulated from a custom transformed into a statutory right. It relied on S.S. Munna Lal v. S.S. Rajkumar, Giasi Ram v. Ramjilal, Commissioner of Wealth Tax v. Chunder Sen, Yudhishter v. Ashok Kumar, Thakur Gokulchand v. Parvin Kumari, and authorities on the legal character of custom, including Daya Ram v. Sohel Singh and Salig Ram v. Munshi Ram.

predicates.alienation_challenge_proceeding: A proceeding concerns a challenge to an alienation of property.
predicates.customary_alienation_right_recognized: The applicable legal framework had recognized or regulated a customary right to challenge some alienations.
predicates.succession_law_does_not_address_the_rest: The succession rules applicable to the parties did not deal with the relevant restriction on alienation.
predicates.custom_based_challenge_right_later_aboli: A later legal change ended the right to challenge alienations on the ground that they were contrary to custom.

issues.definition: Where a recognized customary challenge right is later abolished but the applicable succession rules did not address the restriction, the customary right ends while independent Hindu-law rights remain.

issues.legal_issue: An appellate court must consider an independent Hindu-law basis for challenging an alienation when the lower courts did not decide it and the appellants wish to pursue it.
material_facts: The appellants' cases had not been considered by the lower courts under Hindu law.
The custom-based ground was no longer available under the 1973 amendment.
The Court identified appellants who were willing to pursue their cases under Hindu law and directed that those cases be examined, with further evidence permitted if needed.
issues.conclusion: The cases of the willing appellants were sent back to the High Court to examine their claims under Hindu law after hearing the parties and, if needed, allowing further necessary evidence.
issues.legal_principle: The ending of a custom-based challenge does not affect independent rights under Hindu law. Because those claims had not been examined below, they required consideration on remand. The Court applied section 4 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, as limited to matters dealt with by that Act, and the principle that the parties' rights under Hindu law remained unaffected by abolition of the customary challenge. It relied on the succession-law authorities including S.S. Munna Lal v. S.S. Rajkumar, Giasi Ram v. Ramjilal, Commissioner of Wealth Tax v. Chunder Sen, and Yudhishter v. Ashok Kumar.
